content:
According to Bloomberg, U.S. bipartisan senators are urging Apple CEO Tim Cook to commit by August 21 that the company will not use memory chips from Chinese suppliers ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) and Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC). The full report follows below.

Background

Apple is trying to cope with an ongoing memory chip shortage and has reportedly been seeking approval from the Trump administration to source components from ChangXin Memory Technologies and Yangtze Memory Technologies; both companies have been designated as Chinese military companies by the U.S. Department of Defense.

Legally, Apple does not need U.S. government approval to purchase chips from these companies, but if it proceeds without government backing, the company could face significant political consequences.

As a result, Apple CEO Tim Cook, in an interview with The Wall Street Journal just before its latest price hike, said that "all options should be on the table," and added that "we should consider all sources of supply."

In the days that followed, The Wall Street Journal reported that Apple has been seeking government assurances to allow it to purchase chips from ChangXin Memory Technologies, while the Financial Times reported that Apple is in talks with Yangtze Memory Technologies to purchase chips. The Financial Times later further reported that Apple is testing DRAM chips from ChangXin Memory Technologies.

Previously, The Wall Street Journal had reported that Apple's use of Chinese memory chips may not be limited to the Chinese market, and that the company is seeking government approval to use components from ChangXin Memory Technologies and Yangtze Memory Technologies in products sold outside the United States.

The report also detailed that Micron is actively lobbying the government to reject Apple's request, on the grounds that allowing Chinese suppliers into Apple's supply chain could weaken U.S. domestic memory production.

This is not the first time Apple has tried to purchase memory chips from Yangtze Memory Technologies. In 2022, the company had studied using components from that supplier in some iPhones sold in China, but the plan was shelved after it drew the attention of U.S. lawmakers and as export controls tightened.

At the time, Senator Marco Rubio, who also serves as vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, accused Apple of "playing with fire," and other lawmakers from both parties also warned that the deal could pose a national security risk.

Lawmakers Renew Pressure

Bloomberg reported today that "a group of U.S. bipartisan senators are urging Apple to abandon any move to purchase chips from blacklisted Chinese semiconductor suppliers (ChangXin Memory Technologies) and (Yangtze Memory Technologies), warning that the iPhone maker faces the risk of relying on a hostile nation for critical components."

According to the report, the lawmakers described Apple's plans as "short-sighted," and said the move would "ensure that the world's most valuable consumer electronics company becomes increasingly dependent on a supplier formally designated by the U.S. government as a Chinese military company for critical components."

The lawmakers also noted that other companies may follow Apple's lead, potentially harming U.S. domestic memory production as well as planned investment projects in states such as Indiana, Idaho, New York, and Virginia.

They added that any initial restrictions limiting ChangXin Memory Technologies' memory chips to products sold in China would be difficult to maintain, because "once a component passes Apple's production qualification, promoting it to global use is just a procurement decision away."

Finally, in addition to requiring Apple to commit by August 21 to "avoid using memory from ChangXin Memory Technologies or Yangtze Memory Technologies in its products," the senators also asked Apple to provide details of any data shared with ChangXin Memory Technologies during the component qualification process, and pointed out that the transfer of controlled technical data to advanced Chinese chip manufacturing facilities may require approval from the Department of Commerce.

Apple did not immediately respond to Bloomberg's request for comment.
